title: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Pricing: 2026 Price Guide
summary: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure pricing varies by service and region. Find current rates and a sample bill to estimate your expenses.
body_markdown:
## Hidden OCI costs and billing limits


When you doubled your inputs, outbound data was the line most likely to have moved. OCI gives you **10 TB a month free** , then meters every gigabyte after that at $0.0085.


Licences, support and commitments sit on top of the metered lines.


### OCI egress costs and free outbound data


Nothing is charged for the first 10 TB each month; the meter's gigabytes leaving Oracle's network. At $0.0085 per GB, a team serving 10 TB pays $0 and one serving 50 TB pays $348.16. One serving 100 TB pays $783.36, according to[RateCard](https://ratecard.cloud/egress/) .


Check the arithmetic against your own traffic. Going from 50 to 100 TB adds $435.20, so each further 10 TB costs about $87.


The risk, according to[Ratecard](https://ratecard.cloud/egress/) , is that the 10 TB allowance's the only protection for a small team, so estimate monthly outbound volume before you sign.


Egress isn't the only line that scales with use. Block volumes bill for performance units as well as capacity, so a database volume tuned for high throughput costs more than the same size at the default setting.


Each load balancer and each reserved public IP that sits unattached still appears on the invoice.


### OCI licence, support and commitment costs


It is licences that turn a cheap compute price into an expensive one. Running Oracle Database or other Oracle software on OCI can add a licence charge per processor-hour, and bringing your own licence only helps if you already own enough of them.


Second comes support. The tier you pick sets your response times, and on some plans it's billed as a share of your monthly spend, so the support line grows with the rest of the bill.


A small team should price the cheapest tier that gives a named contact for production outages and leave the rest.


In return for a lower rate, commitments cost you flexibility. A prepaid or annual commitment lowers the unit price, but you pay for the committed amount whether or not you use it. Commit only to the baseline you're sure of, and leave bursts on pay-as-you-go.


### Service limits, quotas and idle reclamation


On day one, every new tenancy starts with service limits on how many instances, volumes and load balancers you can create in a region.


Quotas work the other way: an administrator can cap a compartment's spending or resource count, which stops a runaway test from becoming a surprise bill. Set them on every non-production compartment.


A cap or an alert only helps if someone sees it, and[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) can pass an OCI budget alert on to a Slack channel or an email list.


It bills a run at 1 credit whether the flow has two steps or ten, where Zapier bills per task and Make per module, so splitting the alert into a lookup, a filter and a message costs nothing extra.


On the free plan, which is $0 with 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows, a weekly cost report uses about four or five credits a month.


Third, idle reclamation. Oracle can reclaim Always Free compute instances it judges idle, so a side project left quiet may vanish. Do not host anything you can't rebuild on a free instance.
